explain.headline: Clean Air Needs Targets, Timelines and Accountability in India
static: The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) was launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in 2019 as a national strategy to tackle air pollution.
NCAP initially aimed to reduce PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations by 20 to 30 percent by 2024, later revised to achieve a 40 percent reduction by 2026 in target cities.
The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) is a set of emergency measures implemented in Delhi-NCR corresponding to different levels of air quality severity.
Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan is an initiative by the Central Pollution Control Board to rank cities based on implementation of clean air action plans.
Air pollution in India is governed primarily under the umbrella of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981.
explain.what: The editorial argues that India must transition from administrative compliance to measurable air quality improvements by establishing clear targets, timelines, and interdepartmental accountability.
explain.why_in_news: The persistent poor air quality in Indian cities despite initiatives like NCAP and GRAP has brought the structural flaws of clean-air governance into focus.
explain.background: Current air quality policies suffer from a focus on administrative tasks rather than pollution reduction, fragmented institutional responsibilities, and a lack of performance-linked funding.
significance: Highlights the massive economic loss of 10% of regional GDP in South Asia due to air pollution health and productivity impacts.
Demonstrates the need to reform urban air ranking systems to prioritize particulate matter reduction over routine administrative chores.
Provides actionable recommendations including performance-linked central grants and integrated multi-sectoral planning.
prelims: Actual reductions in particulate matter account for 2.5 per cent of a city’s total score in Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan.
The national standard for annual average PM10 level is 60 micrograms per cubic metre.
Lucknow annual average PM10 level declined to around 135 micrograms per cubic metre.
Every rupee invested in climate and clean-air measures can generate 21 rupees in economic and health benefits according to UNEP and Climate and Clean Air Coalition.
explain.mains: India’s clean-air policy needs clear targets, fixed timelines and accountability rather than merely administrative measures. Discuss the challenges in achieving clean air and suggest measures to improve the effectiveness of India’s clean-air policy.

texts.x: Source: The post “Clean air needs targets, timelines and accountability” has been created based on “Clean air needs targets, timelines and accountability” published in “Indian Express” on 28th September 2026. UPSC Syllabus: GS 3- Environment Context: Air pollution threatens public health and economic productivity in India. Despite initiatives like NCAP and GRAP, air quality remains…

points: Air pollution heavily threatens public health and economic productivity across India despite existing frameworks like NCAP and GRAP.
The Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan rankings focus heavily on administrative activities, where actual pollution reduction accounts for only 2.5% of a city score.
Lucknow annual average PM10 level declined from 253 micrograms per cubic metre in 2017-18 to 135, but it remains twice the national standard of 60.
Delhi has shown no appreciable improvement in winter air quality over the last four years despite Graded Response Action Plan measures.
South Asia loses 10% of its regional GDP annually due to reduced productivity and healthcare costs from air pollution.
Fragmented institutional responsibilities across multiple ministries and agencies create coordination problems and weaken accountability.
Meeting national air quality standards in Delhi and NCR from 2026 can cut cumulative PM2.5 exposure burden by 20% by 2040.
The author proposes setting clear targets, measuring actual outcomes, fixing accountability, linking funding with performance, and reforming NCAP 2.0.
sum.text:
Context: Air pollution threatens public health and economic productivity in India. Despite initiatives like NCAP and GRAP, air quality remains poor in several cities. Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan focuses mainly on administrative activities, while actual pollution reduction accounts for only 2.5% of a city’s score. In this context, it is important that India must move beyond fragmented measures and focus on clear targets, fixed timelines, interdepartmental coordination and accountability.
Focus on administrative activities: The Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan rankings assess activities such as road sweeping, waste management, sidewalk paving and action-plan preparation. Actual reductions in particulate matter account for only 2.5 per cent of a city’s total score.
Limited improvement in air quality: Lucknow’s annual average PM10 level has declined from 253 micrograms per cubic metre in 2017–18 to around 135, but it remains more than twice the national standard of 60 micrograms per cubic metre.
Ineffective pollution-control measures: Delhi has shown no appreciable improvement in winter air quality over the last four years, despite pollution-control measures and activities under the Graded Response Action Plan.
High economic and health costs: According to an assessment by UNEP and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition, South Asia loses the equivalent of 10 per cent of its regional GDP annually due to reduced productivity and healthcare costs associated with air pollution.
Fragmented institutional responsibilities : Transport, electricity generation, industry, waste management, agriculture and household cooking contribute to air pollution. Their management by different ministries and agencies creates coordination problems and weakens accountability.
Economic losses due to delays: If Delhi and the NCR meet national air quality standards on schedule from 2026, their cumulative PM2.5 exposure burden could decline by 20 per cent by 2040. An eight-year delay would halve this reduction.
Set clear targets and timelines: The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) should establish measurable pollution-reduction targets and fixed deadlines for every responsible agency.
Measure actual outcomes: The government should assess clean-air programmes based on reductions in pollution exposure and the speed at which people receive relief, rather than administrative activities alone.
Fix institutional accountability: The government should clearly define the responsibilities of ministries, departments…

static: Theatre commands integrate the resources of the Army, Navy, and Air Force under a single commander to fight wars as a unified force.
The creation of Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) was a major step recommended by the Kargil Review Committee to facilitate theaterisation.
Unlike the current single-service commands, integrated commands look at a specific geographical theater of conflict rather than individual services.
India currently has 17 single-service commands and only two joint commands (Andaman and Nicobar Command and Strategic Forces Command).
Major global militaries like the US, China, Russia, and France already operate under fully integrated theatre command systems.

explain.headline: When Tiger Reserve Boundaries Go Wrong, Wildlife and People Pay the Price
static: Tiger reserves in India are governed under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, specifically Section 38V which provides for core or critical tiger habitats and buffer or peripheral areas.
Core areas are kept inviolate for tiger conservation without settling of rights, while buffer areas promote co-existence and support wildlife movement alongside human activities.
National parks and wildlife sanctuaries enjoy high statutory protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, distinct from the administrative buffer definitions of tiger reserves.
The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) is a statutory body established under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for implementing Project Tiger.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 as a centrally sponsored scheme to ensure a viable population of Bengal tigers in their natural habitats.
explain.what: The editorial discusses the administrative and ecological confusion caused by overlapping boundaries and erroneous classifications between tiger reserve buffers, wildlife sanctuaries, and national parks.
explain.why_in_news: The Standing Committee of Karnataka's State Board for Wildlife decided on October 5 to review and rationalise tiger reserve buffers using a technical committee.
explain.background: Tiger reserves comprise core habitats and peripheral buffers, but overlapping designations with pre-existing wildlife sanctuaries and national parks have led to regulatory confusion and community hardships.
significance: Highlights the friction between rigorous wildlife conservation laws and the socio-economic welfare of local forest communities.
Exposes administrative lapses and approval inconsistencies by central bodies like the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA).
Emphasizes the need for scientific assessment, meaningful stakeholder consultation, and transparent boundary rationalisation.
prelims: Section 38V(4) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 defines core and buffer areas of tiger reserves.
Nugu Wildlife Sanctuary forms part of Bandipur Tiger Reserve's buffer.
Dandeli Wildlife Sanctuary and Anshi National Park are included in Kali Tiger Reserve's buffer.

The decision is significant because portions of existing wildlife sanctuaries and national parks across Karnataka have been notified as tiger reserve buffers, raising concerns about wildlife protection, conservation management and the welfare of communities living within these landscapes.
A tiger reserve comprises a core or critical tiger habitat, prioritised for conservation, and a surrounding buffer supporting wildlife movement alongside legitimate human activities.
Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks already enjoy statutory protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Overlapping designations can create confusion over applicable rules, management priorities and restrictions imposed on residents.
Section 38V(4), Explanation (i) and (ii), of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, defines core or critical tiger habitats and buffer or peripheral areas. Reiterating these statutory distinctions, the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), further clarified in May 2009 that buffer areas are peripheral to core habitats and do not have the status of wildlife sanctuaries or national parks.
Yet portions of these protected areas have been included in buffers. That NTCA continues approving tiger reserve proposals apparently inconsistent with its own explicit clarifications, despite being entrusted with implementing Section 38V, raises serious questions about its responsibility, consistency, and accountability.
In Karnataka, Nugu Wildlife Sanctuary forms part of Bandipur Tiger Reserve’s buffer. points: The article examines how the 42nd Constitutional Amendment of 1976 permanently centralised India's federal architecture.
Indira Gandhi pushed the amendment through a self-extended Lok Sabha during the Emergency while opposition leaders were jailed.
Acting on the Swaran Singh Committee, the amendment shifted subjects like education, forests, and administration of justice into the Concurrent List.
It also inserted Entry 2A into the Union List, enabling armed forces deployment in states without request, and froze Lok Sabha seat allocation based on the 1971 Census.
Although the 44th Amendment removed Article 257A regarding armed forces, it left the transfer of education, forests, and court administration intact.
Subsequent centralisation continues through executive tools like UGC regulations mandating nominee inclusion for vice-chancellor selections and conditional PM-SHRI grants.
With the delimitation freeze ending after the upcoming census, southern states now face the threat of losing parliamentary representation.
The author proposes placing the Seventh Schedule changes before the Inter-State Council under Article 263 to consult states before redrawing the map.
sum.text:
On November 2, 1976, the Lok Sabha passed the Constitution (42nd Amendment) Bill by 366 votes to four. Opposition leaders such as Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, and LK Advani had been jailed under the Emergency, and the House was sitting on a self-extended term. Indira Gandhi called the amendment “responsive to the aspirations of the people and reflects the realities of the present time and the future.” Remembered for adding “socialist” and “secular” to the Preamble, the “mini-Constitution” left a far less discussed mark on India’s federal architecture.
Today’s Union-state disputes over the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), vice-chancellor appointments, and delimitation — all trace back to 1976. The Janata government repaired the Emergency’s damage to civil liberties but left its damage to federalism in place, making the 42nd Amendment the most durable instrument of centralisation in our Constitution. Acting on the Swaran Singh Committee’s recommendations, the amendment moved five subjects out of the State List.
Education (Entry 11) was folded into Entry 25 of the Concurrent List. Forests and the protection of wild animals and birds became Entries 17A and 17B, weights and measures became Entry 33A, and the administration of justice and the constitution of courts below the High Courts became Entry 11A. Entry 2A of the Union List and Article 257A empowered the Union to deploy its armed forces in any state without its request.
The allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and the state assemblies was frozen on the basis of the 1971 Census. The states sought none of this, and the ratification required under the proviso to Article 368(2) came in a year when the Union had already dismissed the DMK government in Tamil Nadu under Article 356, on January 31, 1976. The Janata Party went to the polls in 1977 promising to “restore the Constitution to the condition it was in before the Emergency”.
The 44th Amendment deleted Article 257A that empowered the Union to deploy armed forces in states for law and order maintenance. Yet no amendment returned education, forests, or the administration of justice to the states, and Entry 2A remains in the Union List to this day. The Sarkaria Commission later recommended consultation with the states on Concurrent List subjects but it has rarely happened.
Nowhere is the legacy of 1976 sharper than in education. Even before the transfer, Entry 66 of the Union List let Parliament coordinate and determine…

points: Microsoft has made a voluntary exit offer to as many as 60,000 of its staff, representing 27 per cent of its total workforce.
The move affects employees spread across the US, Canada, the UK, and India, following an earlier voluntary retirement programme in July.
The underlying reason for these massive layoffs is the advent of artificial intelligence, allowing companies to do more with fewer employees.
Technology firms are freeing up capital to invest hundreds of billions of dollars into building AI infrastructure despite continued profit growth.
Other major players across technology and banking, including Barclays, HSBC, Oracle, Meta, and Amazon, have also shed significant workforce parts.
The immediate global restructuring impact will hit Indian IT companies, posing medium-term headwinds for India's largest white-collar job provider.
AI's job-replacement threat creates a major challenge for Indian policymakers struggling to create quality jobs amid youth population bulges.
sum.text:
Microsoft (MS), the technology company synonymous with computers and software, has made a “ voluntary exit offer ” to as many as 60,000 of its staff. Its Chief People Officer said that it “gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support”. “With support” suggests that those who do not take up the offer may face a future scenario where they may be let go of, but without the monetary compensation that is available now. The move affects 27 per cent of MS’s total workforce spread across the US, Canada, the UK and India. This comes on the back of a “voluntary retirement programme” in July that was offered to more than 8,700 employees. More than 30 per cent of them accepted it even as MS followed it up by firing another 4,800 a few weeks later.
While it was not stated openly, a reason for these layoffs is the advent of artificial intelligence. Companies like MS are finding, one, that with the power of AI by their side, they can do more with fewer employees. And two, that there is a need to free up money so that hundreds of billions of dollars more can be invested into building AI infrastructure. MS is neither the first company nor the only one that is cutting employees in the wake of AI. Reportedly, some of the biggest players across technology and banking — Barclays, HSBC, Oracle, Meta, Amazon, to name a few — have shed significant bits of their workforce in 2026. What’s more, companies are doing it even as their profits continue to grow.
The immediate impact of AI-related restructuring at the global scale will also be felt by Indian IT companies. It is possible that, in the short term, the transition to AI will create some job opportunities, but over the medium term, this industry, which is the largest provider of white-collar jobs in India, will likely face headwinds. The bigger challenge, however, is for Indian policymakers. AI’s much-touted ability to replace humans threatens India at a time when the country is experiencing a bulge in its youth population, while struggling to create good quality jobs, amid growing unrest among the young. These trends should make policymakers rethink their human resource strategies.

Draft National Steel Policy Vision 2047, released on Oct 10, envisages nearly tripling steelmaking capacity, with the coal-based blast-furnace route accounting for 55% of steel production. This pathway could lock in ~$1.5 tn in additional coking coal imports over the plants' lifetime. Coking coal can account for ~40% of cost of producing a tonne of steel, leaving steelmakers vulnerable to rising international coal prices and disruptions to freight. That exposure creates a direct risk for downstream industries that use steel. India imports 92% of coking coal its steelmakers need, at prices set in dollars. Blast furnaces need this coal to turn iron ore into iron. The policy projects annual demand more than tripling from 72 mn tonnes today to 236 mn tonnes by 2047. The coal ministry's roadmap would increase domestic coking coal supply from about 6 mn tonnes today to 23 mn tonnes by 2030. If supply remains at that level thereafter, India will still need to import about 213 mn tonnes annually by 2047. At the $236-a-tonne benchmark average for Jan-July 2026, that represents about $50 bn a year before freight. Every $10 increase in coal price would add another $2.1 bn to the annual bill. Competition from inexpensive Chinese steel limits Indian mills' ability to pass on higher costs, squeezing their margins and potentially reducing the money available for expansion. Implications extend beyond steelworks. Construction and infrastructure consume 67% of India's steel. Volatile steel prices can raise the cost of public projects and housing. Smaller manufacturers buying steel for machinery and components also need predictable input costs to price orders and invest. India's steel expansion should, therefore, reduce dependence on imported coal and make production costs more predictable. sum.text:
BARELY 24 hours after the Road Transport Ministry notified changes in the Central Motor Vehicles Rules to permit flex-fuel vehicles designed for E100 (nearly pure ethanol), the Petroleum Ministry has stated that there is no immediate plan to increase ethanol blending beyond 20%. Perhaps the government should think its own potentially good idea through before manifesting an embarrassing flip-flop. The E100 move promises reduced dependence on imported crude oil, but it raises questions about affordability, infrastructure and the long-term ethanol policy.
Without reliable supplies, car buyers may find themselves paying for advanced technology that they cannot conveniently use. Moreover, conventional petrol vehicles cannot safely use E85 (85% ethanol, 15% petrol) or E100 unless specifically designed and certified for these blends. Clear communication and adequate consumer protection are therefore essential.
The distinction between authorising the use of technology and changing the national blending target must be explained clearly to dispel doubts. Also, ethanol expansion should not come at the cost of food security. The exclusion of sugar-based ethanol from the 2026-27 procurement tender reflects concerns over domestic sugar availability.
Greater reliance on maize and rice, meanwhile, demands careful assessment of food supplies, agricultural prices, water use and pressure on land resources. Claims of savings on oil imports must be weighed against these costs. India should pursue ethanol innovation, but not treat it as a universal solution.
Transparent fuel pricing, independent vehicle performance assessments and dependable distribution networks must accompany regulatory changes. Whether E100 becomes widely beneficial will depend less on what the rules permit than on how responsibly the policy is implemented and how effectively public trust is built.

sum.text:
The Election Commission of India (ECI)’s affidavit in the Supreme Court highlights the consensus and unanimity behind the poll body’s decisions, and argues that its intentions behind ordering both the special intensive revision (SIR) and several changes in the contentious exercise were honourable and in line with its constitutional remit. The reply, which goes some way towards clarifying the motives of the body, leaves key procedural changes unexplained. On SIR, the affidavit says all decisions were taken unanimously by three election commissioners (ECs) and that suggestions, queries, or objections during deliberations didn’t count as decisions.
It clarifies that letters by two ECs to the cabinet secretary concerned an internal work order that was never implemented after another July 30 decision. On the question of motive, ECI presents a credible case. But it never answers procedural queries around who ordered the changes, whether objections raised by ECs were addressed, or how the constant tweaks in SIR procedure evolved.
On Form 6, the statutory application used for enrolling new voters, ECI said the additional declaration was a separate document, and not a modification of the requirements laid down under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. But its admission that the way it appeared online “could be construed as though an amendment of Form 6 had been made” and that “certain steps taken by the officers” needed “to be corrected” raises more questions, especially against the backdrop of earlier ECI communication that said the “declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court”. This newspaper has reported that the declaration before the apex court was a different one.
On West Bengal, ECI admitted that the state chief electoral officer (CEO) filed 1.6 million appeals before judicial tribunals to delete voters. But it doesn’t answer who authorised these appeals or whether each case — already cleared by a judicial officer — was individually evaluated. Motives are important (apart from being the focus of protests and legal challenges by the opposition parties).

For a gargantuan exercise such as SIR, procedural hardships can make the difference between holding the right to vote and losing it. The country has a unicameral (single-house) parliament with 120 members, elected nationally every four years. Three main branches of power: Legislature (Knesset).
Executive (PM holds executive power). Judiciary (headed by the Supreme Court, interprets Basic Laws and reviews legislation). The government depends on the Knesset’s confidence and must maintain a working majority (at least 61 seats) to govern.

sum.text:
Cyclone Arnab strengthened rapidly before crossing the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts. Warm seas, ocean heat and favourable atmospheric conditions supported its intensification. El Niño can influence cyclone formation and tracks through changing wind patterns.
Cyclone Arnab gathered strength over the Bay of Bengal, advanced towards Andhra Pradesh faster than expected and retained its intensity for hours after reaching the coast. Its development brought together the conditions that can make a cyclone strengthen quickly: warm seas, heat stored beneath the surface and an atmosphere that allows the storm’s circulation to organise. Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts early on Wednesday, October 28, as a very severe cyclonic storm, uprooting trees and electricity poles and disrupting power supply.
More than 1,80,000 people were evacuated across Andhra Pradesh and Odisha before its arrival. The storm later weakened into a severe cyclonic storm. But its rapid strengthening and changing movement have raised questions about the role of El Niño and the difficulty of forecasting sudden changes in cyclone intensity.
How Arnab Grew Into A Very Severe CycloneArnab began as a low-pressure system over the southeast Bay of Bengal on October 23. By October 26, it had developed into a cyclonic storm before strengthening through the severe and very severe categories. It was the first cyclone of 2026 in the North Indian Ocean basin, which comprises the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.
As the storm approached land faster than initially expected, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) revised its landfall forecast late on Tuesday, bringing the expected crossing forward from the forenoon to the early hours of Wednesday. Arnab crossed between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam with sustained winds of 125–135 kmph, gusting to 140 kmph. Its outer rainbands had already begun moving over land before the centre reached the coast.
The system did not immediately lose strength. It maintained its intensity for at least six hours before weakening into a severe cyclonic storm. According to IMD, it remained nearly stationary close to Narsapur and Yanam from around 4 am, slowing the crossing process.

points: A newly released US intelligence report has provided a rare high-resolution satellite image of China's secretive Shenlong spaceplane in orbit.
The image, captured in 2024 by a Vantor satellite from 90 kilometres away, shows a winged vehicle with open payload bay doors and another spacecraft attached.
China's spaceplane is an uncrewed, reusable vehicle designed to travel into orbit and return to Earth by gliding towards a runway.
China launched its first experimental reusable spacecraft in September 2020, with subsequent missions lasting 276 days, nine months, and a fourth starting in February 2026.
The open payload bay and the attached spacecraft suggest the vehicle can deploy equipment, release smaller objects, or conduct proximity operations.
Rendezvous and proximity operations involve manoeuvring close to other spacecraft for civilian servicing or potential military interference.
Both China and the US, which operates the comparable X-37B vehicle, maintain secrecy, creating uncertainty over whether the missions are civilian or military.
The capabilities demonstrated by reusable spaceplanes have significant implications for the security and protection of space infrastructure.
sum.text: New Delhi: For years, China has kept the activities of its secretive spaceplane under wraps, offering little more than brief official statements about its missions. Now, a newly released US intelligence report has offered a rare glimpse of the spacecraft in orbit, using a high-resolution satellite image that captures details Beijing has not publicly explained. The image, included in a US Defense Intelligence Agency report published on 26 October, shows a winged, shuttle-like vehicle with its payload bay doors open and another spacecraft attached to its rear section. It was captured in 2024 by a satellite operated by Vantor, formerly known as Maxar Technologies, from a distance of around 90 kilometres. The spacecraft is widely believed to be China’s Shenlong, or “Divine Dragon”, an uncrewed vehicle designed to travel into orbit and return to Earth. Beijing has disclosed few details about its missions, leaving researchers to piece together its activities from satellite-tracking data and observations. Show Full Article So what can the photograph tell us, and why are space experts paying attention? What is China’s spaceplane? Unlike conventional satellites, which generally remain in orbit, a spaceplane combines features of a spacecraft and an aircraft. It is launched into space aboard a rocket, operates in orbit and can return to Earth by gliding towards a runway. The ability to reuse the vehicle could reduce the cost of repeated missions and allow equipment to be recovered, examined and tested on the ground. It could also enable experiments that would be difficult or expensive to conduct using conventional satellites. China launched its first experimental reusable spacecraft in September 2020. Its second mission lasted 276 days, while the third, launched in December 2023, ended in September 2024 after about nine months in orbit. A fourth mission began in February 2026. Chinese state media has described the programme as a test of reusable spacecraft technology intended to support the peaceful use of space, without disclosing the specific experiments being conducted. The US operates a comparable uncrewed vehicle, the X-37B, which is used for classified experiments and technology testing. Both programmes illustrate the growing interest in spacecraft that can stay in orbit for extended periods before returning to Earth. Also Read: Spain built a high-speed rail giant. Union Cabinet has allocated Rs 7,395 crore for the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Gram Swaraj Yojana. This scheme will promote local-level capacity building and resource management for panchayats across India. Elected representatives will receive training to enhance their governance capabilities and local planning efforts. The initiative aims to financially empower panchayats through better utilization of available resources. Implementation will occur from 2026-27 to 2030-31, aligning with the Sixteenth Finance Commission period.

The Union Cabinet has approved the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Gram Swaraj Yojana for 2026-27 to 2030-31, with an outlay of ₹7,395.55 crore. The scheme will cover over 2.55 lakh Panchayats and traditional local bodies, benefiting around 32 lakh elected representatives and functionaries.
The scheme aims to strengthen grassroots governance by enabling panchayats to plan development around local needs, resources and financial priorities

points: The Union Cabinet approved the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Gram Swaraj Yojana with a total financial outlay of Rs 7,395.55 crore.
The scheme aims to shift from traditional prescription-based schemes to empowering panchayats for decentralised planning based on local resources.
It will run from 2026-27 to 2030-31, coinciding with the Sixteenth Finance Commission period.
The Centre will contribute Rs 4,869.48 crore and states will provide Rs 2,526.07 crore towards the total outlay.
Around 32 lakh elected representatives, panchayat functionaries, and stakeholders across more than 2.55 lakh panchayats will receive annual training.
The programme supports the preparation of holistic Gram Panchayat Development Plans each year through the eGramSwaraj portal.
It promotes transparency and better fund utilisation through online audits on AuditOnline and aims to boost own-source revenue.
State governments and UT administrations will handle implementation under a Central Empowered Committee without creating permanent posts.
sum.text:
<p>New Delhi: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Gram Swaraj Yojana with an outlay of Rs 7,395.55 crore, marking a major push to strengthen rural local bodies through capacity building and decentralised planning.<br><br><a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/ashwini-vaishnaw">Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw</a> told media that the initiative as a “paradigm change” from traditional prescription-based schemes to one that empowers panchayats to identify local resources and constraints and prepare development plans suited to their needs. The Panchayati Raj Ministry termed it a next-generation governance reform aligned with the vision of Viksit Bharat.<br><br>The scheme will run from 2026-27 to 2030-31, coinciding with the Sixteenth Finance Commission period. Of the total outlay, the Centre will contribute Rs 4,869.48 crore and states Rs 2,526.07 crore.</p>.Old before rich: 20% of India's population to be over 60 by 2050.<p>Around 32 lakh elected representatives, panchayat functionaries and other stakeholders across more than 2.55 lakh panchayats and traditional local bodies will benefit from annual training to enhance local planning, resource management and citizen engagement.<br><br>The programme will support preparation of 2.55 lakh holistic Gram Panchayat Development Plans each year through the eGramSwaraj portal, improve fund utilisation, and promote transparency via online audits on AuditOnline.
It also aims to boost panchayats’ own-source revenue for greater financial self-reliance and will reach at least one crore citizens in each awareness drive through gram sabhas and digital platforms.<br><br>Implementation will be handled by state governments and Union Territory administrations under the oversight of a Central Empowered Committee. No permanent posts will be created, a statement said.</p>

sum.text:
India and Mexico will sign terms of reference this week to formally launch negotiations for a free trade deal, aiming to shield exports of Indian automobiles, textiles, footwear, plastic, steel, chemicals and toys from recently-imposed high tariffs in the Mexican market, officials familiar with the details said.
Both India and Mexico have already finalised terms of reference (ToR) for a preferential trade agreement (PTA). The two sides will formally sign the ToR in the next couple of days as commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal is visiting Mexico from Monday, they said, asking not to be named. Agrawal is on a week-long trade mission covering Mexico and Brussels, headquarters of the European Union.
The proposed India-Mexico PTA is expected to shield Indian exporters from high tariffs up to 50% imposed by the Mexican government on 1,463 items on imports from countries with which it does not have any bilateral deal such as a PTA or a free trade agreement (FTA).
Experts said the ToR is the first step towards shielding Indian exporters from high tariffs in Mexico, particularly Indian automobile exports to the country. According to the government trade data, out of total $5.73 billion Indian merchandise exports to Mexico in 2025-26, automobiles constituted the single largest segment at $1.92 billion.
The identified items include goods such as automobiles, textiles, clothing, plastic, steel, household appliances, aluminium, toys, furniture, footwear, leather goods, paper and cardboard, motorcycles, trailers, and glass products.

The Union Cabinet has approved the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme with an outlay of Rs 1,856.67 crore for 2026-27 to 2033-34, aiming to boost investment, manufacturing, innovation and exports in the sports goods sector and strengthen India's position in global supply chains. Announced in the Union Budget 2026-27, the scheme seeks to build a globally competitive sports goods industry through support for investment, technology adoption, research and development, skill development, quality certification and market access. It is aligned with the goals of Khelo Bharat Niti 2025, Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
A major component of the scheme is the creation of Sports Goods Manufacturing Zones (SGMZs), which will promote cluster-based manufacturing by bringing together manufacturers, suppliers, testing facilities, design and prototyping centres, and ancillary units. These zones will be developed through convergence with infrastructure available under the BHAVYA Scheme and NICDC industrial parks, with the aim of improving efficiency, strengthening industry linkages and enhancing competitiveness, the government said on Wednesday.
The scheme also seeks to attract fresh investments and expand domestic manufacturing capacity. Under the Anchor Investment Support component, leading domestic and global manufacturers, brands and retail chains will be encouraged to set up units within SGMZs. The Turnover Linked Support component will incentivise higher production and capacity expansion. Together, these two interventions have been allocated Rs 1,130 crore and are expected to help reduce import dependence, increase domestic value addition, attract private investment and generate employment.
Recognising the role of MSMEs in the sector, the scheme will support the modernisation of existing sports goods manufacturing clusters through the development of common facilities and shared infrastructure.
To improve quality standards, manufacturers will receive assistance for obtaining and renewing certifications from international sports federations. An allocation of Rs 105 crore has been earmarked for this purpose, which is expected to help Indian products gain wider acceptance in overseas markets, the government added.

Modi is scheduled to visit Gujarat on October 30 and 31.
During an event in Bhildi town, the Prime Minister will disburse the 24th instalment of the PM-Kisan, providing over Rs 18,680 crore to more than 9.34 crore farmer families across the country, the minister said.
In Gujarat, more than 52.33 lakh farmer families will receive financial assistance exceeding Rs 1,051 crore, Vaghani said after reviewing preparations for the 'PM Kisan Utsav Divas' event at Bhildi.
The prime minister will also lay the foundation stones for two compressed biogas (CBG) plants being set up by Banas Dairy in Tharad and Radhanpur.
The Tharad plant will process 75 tonnes of cattle dung daily, while the Radhanpur facility will have a processing capacity of 100 tonnes per day.
With the addition of these two plants, the number of Bio-CNG plants under the Banas Model will increase to six, with a combined cattle dung processing capacity of 515 tonnes per day.
Bio-CNG produced from cattle dung is sold at subsidised rates, with Banaskantha Dairy currently supplying around 6,100 kg daily. The six plants are estimated to prevent between 33,400 and 34,600 tonnes of carbon emissions annually.
During the October 30 event, Modi will also inaugurate the Bharat Bovine Breeding and Research Centre (BBBRC), developed at a cost of Rs 328.77 crore, Vaghani said.
The prime minister will also inaugurate Banas Dairy's new potato processing expansion project and its ultra-high-temperature (UHT) facility's automated storage and retrieval system (ASRS).
Under the PM-Kisan scheme, eligible farmer families receive financial assistance of Rs 6,000 annually in three equal instalments.
Vaghani said that more than Rs 4.47 lakh crore had been disbursed nationally through the previous 23 instalments, while over Rs 24,137 crore had been provided to beneficiaries in Gujarat.
To mark the occasion, 34 district-level and more than 2,100 cluster-level events will be organised across Gujarat, with live broadcasts of the main programme.

explain.headline: NHRC Issues Advisory on Protecting Human Rights of Female Inmates and Children
static: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India is a statutory body established on October 12, 1993, under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993.
The NHRC is mandated to protect and promote human rights relating to life, liberty, equality, and dignity of the individual guaranteed by the Constitution.
The Commission consists of a Chairperson who has been a Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court, and other members with knowledge or practical experience in human rights.
The Chairperson and members are appointed by the President of India on the recommendation of a high-powered committee headed by the Prime Minister.
The NHRC has the powers of a civil court trying a suit and can inquire into complaints of human rights violations either suo motu or upon a petition.
While its recommendations are generally advisory in nature, it plays a vital role in highlighting custodial justice, prison reforms, and systemic human rights abuses in India.
explain.what: The National Human Rights Commission has issued a comprehensive advisory to states, Union Territories, and central ministries focusing on the human rights, health, legal aid, and rehabilitation needs of female inmates and their children.
explain.why_in_news: The NHRC issued this advisory to address the vulnerabilities of female prisoners and their children, directing authorities to submit an Action Taken Report within two months.
explain.background: The NHRC is a statutory watchdog set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, tasked with safeguarding human rights and reviewing prison conditions across India.
significance: Highlights the often-overlooked vulnerabilities of women and children inside correctional and custodial facilities.
Pushes for systemic prison reforms by enforcing gender-responsive administrative protocols across all states and union territories.
Ensures institutional accountability by mandating a compliance report within a strict two-month timeframe.
prelims: The advisory focuses on ten broad areas including child database, medical care, and legal aid.
The advisory was sent to nine Union Ministries, Chief Secretaries, and Director Generals of Police.
Authorities are required to furnish an Action Taken Report within two months.

points: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) issued an advisory on the protection of human rights of female inmates and their children.
The advisory emphasizes that female prisoners and their children form a vulnerable group needing focused, gender-responsive attention.
It calls for humane prison conditions, adequate maternal and child healthcare, access to justice, and family preservation.
The advisory covers ten broad areas including arrest and entry, admission records, child database, and mental health services.
Other focus areas include living conditions, hygiene, legal aid, communication, rehabilitation, and foreign national inmates.
The advisory has been sent to nine Union Ministries, Chief Secretaries, and Director Generals of Police of all States and UTs.
The NHRC directed all concerned authorities to implement the recommendations and submit an Action Taken Report within two months.
sum.text:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has issued an advisory on the Protection of Human Rights of Female Inmates and their Children. The advisory emphasises that the rights and needs of prisoners, including female prisoners and their children, require focused attention and a sensitive, gender-responsive approach. The NHRC emphasizes the need to ensure humane prison conditions, adequate healthcare for mothers and children, access to justice, the preservation of family relationships, the protection of children’s best interests, and meaningful opportunities for rehabilitation and social reintegration. The advisory has been issued to nine Union Ministries, Chief Secretaries, and Director Generals of Police of all States and Union Territories.
The Advisory focuses on ten broad areas for action. These include admission records, child database and documentation, Medical care and mental health services, women inmates’ living conditions, hygiene, Legal Aid and Access to Justice. The NHRC has urged all authorities concerned to implement the recommendations in the Advisory and furnish an Action Taken Report within two months.

sum.text:
New Delhi, Oct 27 (IANS) India's ambitions to become a major producer of green hydrogen will be supported by investments of $180 billion-$200 billion through 2030, a report said on Tuesday.
High production costs, limited commissioned capacity, infrastructure gaps and evolving international certification requirements remain significant barriers to large-scale adoption, the report from CARE ESG Ratings Limited said.
Green hydrogen is increasingly being viewed not only as a decarbonisation tool but it is also linked to export competitiveness, energy security and India's ability to establish itself as a competitive producer of low-carbon industrial materials.
The report highlighted that sectors such as steel, fertilisers, refining and chemicals could benefit from green hydrogen push.
Indian steel exporters could face estimated costs of $70–190 per metric tonne on EU-bound shipments, potentially exceeding $270 per metric tonne where default emissions values apply.
The urgency is underscored by the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which could impose carbon-linked costs on exports of emissions-intensive products.
"India's green hydrogen ambitions must translate into commercially viable projects, supported by reliable offtake agreements, competitive production costs and robust infrastructure," said Nikunj Dube, Chief Ratings Officer at CareEdge-ESG.
Green hydrogen currently costs nearly Rs 350–450 per kg, compared with Rs 160–200 per kg for conventional grey hydrogen.
Costs could decline to around $2.4 per kg by 2030 as renewable electricity becomes more competitive, electrolyser costs fall and projects scale up. Until then, adoption will depend partly on policy support, carbon pricing and assured industrial demand.
India consumes approximately 17–19 million metric tonnes of ammonia annually, primarily produced using natural gas. Green ammonia could reduce fossil-fuel import dependence and emissions.
Globally, announced low-emissions hydrogen projects could deliver 27 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa) by 2030, but operational projects, those under construction and those at final investment decision or with a strong likelihood of commissioning account for only slightly more than 6 Mtpa.

explain.headline: High Court Acting Under Section 11 Cannot Extend Arbitrator's Mandate Under Section 29A
static: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is the principal law governing arbitration in India, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law.
Section 11 of the Act provides for the appointment of arbitrators by the Supreme Court or the respective High Court.
Section 29A prescribes time limits for making arbitral awards, mandating conclusion within twelve months from the completion of pleadings.
Section 2(1)(e) defines 'Court' as the principal civil court of original jurisdiction in a district, including the High Court exercising its ordinary original civil jurisdiction.
Amendments to the Arbitration Act over the years have aimed to minimize judicial intervention and expedite institutional and ad-hoc arbitrations in India.
explain.what: The Supreme Court clarified that a High Court exercising powers under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act cannot extend an arbitrator's mandate under Section 29A.
explain.why_in_news: The judgment was delivered to resolve legal confusions regarding the correct judicial forum and procedure for extending an arbitrator's mandate.
explain.background: Section 11 deals with arbitrator appointments, while Section 29A governs time limits for arbitral awards and requires a specific designated 'Court' for extensions.
significance: Prevents jurisdictional overreach by High Courts when dealing with routine administrative appointments versus supervisory extensions.
Enhances procedural predictability in Indian arbitration law by strictly adhering to statutory definitions of the competent court.
Reduces delays caused by filing extension applications in incorrect judicial forums.
prelims: Core holding: Section 11 appointing courts lack suo motu or incidental power to extend mandates under Section 29A.
explain.mains: Examine the scope of judicial intervention under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, with specific reference to the recent Supreme Court ruling on Section 11 and Section 29A.

Addressing the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, Gupta said India's general government debt is projected to decline from 84.3 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 75.1 per cent by 2031-32, even as debt ratios in most advanced and emerging economies are expected to rise. Citing the International Monetary Fund's October 2026 projections, she said global public debt stood at 94 per cent of GDP in 2025 and is expected to cross 100 per cent in 2030, reaching nearly 102 per cent in 2031. The debt trajectory of advanced economies is projected to worsen, with their debt ratio rising from 108.2 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 115.2 per cent in 2031. For emerging market and developing economies, the ratio is expected to increase from 73.7 per cent to 84.2 per cent over the same period. Gupta attributed India's comparatively favourable outlook to fiscal consolidation, strong nominal GDP growth and a lower primary deficit. Nominal GDP growth is projected at around 11 per cent annually, above the effective interest rate on government debt of about 7 per cent, helping keep the debt ratio on a declining path. She also highlighted improvements in the quality of government expenditure, with general government capital expenditure rising to 5.8 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 from around 4 per cent in 2019-20. Higher capital expenditure can help sustain debt by attracting private investment and strengthening the economy's growth potential, she said. Gupta cautioned, however, that the global fiscal environment remains challenging, with rising borrowing costs and elevated debt levels limiting governments' ability to respond to future economic shocks. India's public debt is largely long-term, denominated in domestic currency and held domestically, factors that limit refinancing risks, she said. The RBI Deputy Governor added that India had maintained fiscal prudence while managing external shocks, rather than relying exclusively on fiscal measures to support the economy. (ANI)

New Delhi, Oct 28 (IANS) The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, Ministry of Education and UNESCO have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to introduce clean sport values in classrooms across India through the ‘Sports Values in Every Classroom Toolkit’, in a bid to promote integrity, fairness and respect among school children.
The agreement was exchanged on Wednesday at the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) India’s Clean Sport Conclave in New Delhi, in the presence of Union Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi and UNESCO’s Regional Office for South Asia Director Tim Curtis.
The toolkit will use educational resources and video modules available in 13 Indian languages to reach students nationwide. The initiative aligns with the integration of sports and education emphasised in the Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 and aims to build awareness of clean sport from an early age.
“Sporting excellence and sporting integrity must go hand in hand. Talent, discipline and hard work are essential for sporting success, but integrity, fairness and credibility are equally important,” Mandaviya said, highlighting the need to strengthen clean sport awareness alongside India’s growing sporting ambitions.
The Sports Minister pointed to India’s fourth-place finishes at the Asian Games and Asian Para Games as indicators of the country’s growing sporting strength, while cautioning that doping remained a serious concern requiring sustained efforts in education, prevention, testing and enforcement.
“Supplement testing facilities at National Forensic Sciences University, Gandhinagar and National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research, Hyderabad further help prevent cases of inadvertent doping, while investigations within NADA would be strengthened in line with global practices. The National Anti-Doping Act came into force this year and the government is also preparing to bring provisions for the criminalisation of doping-related activities before Parliament,” Mandaviya added.
Mandaviya further noted that the National Anti-Doping Act had come into force this year, adding that the government was preparing to bring provisions for the criminalisation of doping-related activities before Parliament.

NEW DELHI: The Centre on Wednesday deputed a high-level team to investigation the death of a 19-month-old male Cheetah of Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, caused by firearm pellet injuries. The team has been tasked with undertaking a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to the death of the Cheetah, examining all available evidence and coordinating closely with the Madhya Pradesh forest department to ensure strict and swift action in the matter. The 19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25 in the territorial forests of Morena, outside the protected area of Kuno National Park.
Preliminary medical examinations corroborated multiple internal injuries associated with the firearm pellets. The incident, the first reported casualty of a shooting since PM Narendra Modi launched Project Cheetah at Kuno in Sept, 2022, is being viewed quite seriously at the Centre, given the critical importance of Project Cheetah and the need to ensure the highest standards of protection for the reintroduced population of the Big Cat.“As reported by the MP forest department, the injured cheetah was rescued from the Sheopur Territorial Forest Division the same day and provided intensive veterinary care and emergency surgery at the veterinary facility in Jabalpur. During the surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from its body.
Despite the medical intervention, the Cheetah succumbed to its injuries on Oct 27,” said the Union environment ministry in a statement. It said, “The state govt has already constituted a Special Task Force (STF), comprising forest and police officers, to investigate the incident. sum.text: Allocaecilius Nilgiriensis Latest news Scientists from the Zoological Survey of India have discovered and described a new insect species and named it as Allocaecilius nilgiriensis. About Allocaecilius Nilgiriensis It is a new barklice species, discovered in Nilgiri Hills. It is only the second time a member of this unique barklouse genus has ever been recorded in the country. It brings the total number of known Allocaecilius species worldwide to thirteen. Distribution: It is found across the lush landscapes of the Southern Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu and Keralam. Habitat: These tiny barklice are specialised inhabitants restricted to the damp, shaded canopies and understories of high-altitude shola and evergreen rainforests in the southern Western Ghats. Barklice are a vital microscopic clean-up crew, grazing harmlessly on the surface of tree bark, feeding on mould, fungi, algae, lichens, and dead organic debris Appearance It has distinctive brown patches located in specific distal of its forewings, alongside specialised thumb-like structures on the males lower abdomen (hypandrium) and a deeply indented subgenital plate in females. The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Government of India, has decided to release Rs 1,000 crore in Margin Money (MM) subsidy under the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), promoting self-employment and grassroots entrepreneurship. The subsidy was released by Jitan Ram Manjhi, Union Minister for MSME, during a special event organised by the ministry at Kartavya Bhawan-3, New Delhi. The event was honoured with the presence of high-ranking officials and leaders such as Sushri Shobha Karandlaje, Minister of State for MSME, Shri Bharat Khera, Secretary, Ministry of MSME, other senior officials from the Ministry, CEO, Khadi and Village Industries Commission, CMD, National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC), and the Office of the Development Commissioner (MSME).

The scheme implemented by the Ministry of MSME is carried out nationally by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), with support from other implementing agencies such as KVIBs, District Industries Centres and the Coir Board. The scheme provides financial assistance in the form of MM subsidy on bank-sanctioned project loans for setting up new micro-enterprises to aspiring young entrepreneurs.
To promote long-term enterprise sustainability and growth, KVIC field offices and agencies provide awareness generation, handholding, capacity building, market linkages, monitoring and post-establishment support at grassroots level. PMEGPs remarkable journey since 2014-15 PMEGP has been one of the countrys most successful employment generation programmes. Since FY 2014-15, PMEGP has helped in establishing more than 8.38 lakh micro enterprises through bank-sanctioned loans above Rs 70,000 crore and MM subsidy of Rs 25,193 crore.

sum.text:
MANILA, Philippines — US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth proposed the creation of an "ambitious" new US-Asean defense framework on Wednesday, telling the bloc's leaders it could help them navigate "critically important" years ahead.
The United States has been seeking to boost its regional defense partnerships in recent years, citing the need to uphold what it terms a "free and open Indo-Pacific" as China has increasingly flexed its muscles in the region.
Hegseth, speaking before a meeting with defense chiefs from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) in Cebu, praised what he called the region's "pragmatism" and "proud nationalism."
"We're not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to," he said, calling for cooperation where shared interests overlap.
"As we look to the future in this region, I'd like us to be even more ambitious... we propose that we work together to develop a US-Asean Framework for Defense Cooperation," Hegseth said, without offering details.
"A practical framework that guides our cooperation over the next several years. I will note a critically important next several years."
He added that the United States was ready to begin the project as Singapore assumes the chairmanship of the Asean Defense Ministers' Meeting (ADMM)-Plus in the coming year.
The grouping includes not only the bloc's 11 member states but representatives from the United States, Japan, China, Australia and others.
Hegseth also called for the strengthening of "maritime domain awareness" and advanced cooperation among naval forces.
"These are not symbolic things; they are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do, serious partners train together, learn together, plan together, and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict," he said.
US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the South China Sea.
China's military and coast guard presence in contested areas of the critical waterway nearly doubled in September, Manila said this month.
Japanese defense chief Shinjiro Koizumi met Hegseth on the sidelines of the Cebu event, where they discussed the need to implement "an effective denial defence in the First Island Chain", a reference to islands that lie between China and the open Pacific.
The two allies also committed to continued "close coordination" on munitions production.

sum.text:
India, Oct. 28 -- Indian Naval Ship Sahyadri, an indigenously designed and built guided missile stealth frigate of the Indian Navy, arrived at Busan Naval Harbour, Republic of Korea, on 26 Oct 2026 to participate in the India-Republic of Korea Navy (IN-RoKN) Bilateral Exercise. The visit marks another step towards strengthening maritime cooperation and enhancing interoperability between the two navies in the Indo-Pacific.
INS Sahyadri was accorded a warm welcome by the Republic of Korea Navy (RoKN), reflecting the growing engagement and enduring strategic partnership between India and the Republic of Korea.
During the harbour phase, personnel of both navies will participate in professional interactions, cross-deck visits, cross-training activities and sporting events. These activities will facilitate the exchange of operational experiences and Best Practices, while fostering mutual understanding and professional camaraderie. The Commanding Officer of INS Sahyadri will also call on senior RoKN officials. The harbour phase will be followed by coordinated maritime activities at sea involving INS Sahyadri and ROKS Munmu the Great, providing opportunities to strengthen operational coordination, enhance interoperability and consolidate professional ties between the two navies.
The exercise underscores the shared commitment of India and the Republic of Korea to strengthening maritime cooperation and contributing to peace, stability and security in the Indo-Pacific. It also reflects the Indian Navy's continued efforts to build enduring partnerships with friendly foreign navies through professional engagement and operational cooperation.

sum.text: New Delhi, October 28 (IANS): Union Minister of State (MoS) for AYUSH and Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare Prataprao Jadhav launched the fourth edition of Tobacco-Free Youth Campaign (TFYC 4.0) in the national capital on Wednesday and called for a nationwide movement to protect young people from tobacco use and nicotine addiction. The 60-day pan-India campaign seeks to prevent tobacco initiation among young people, encourage tobacco cessation, strengthen enforcement of tobacco control laws and promote tobacco-free environments across the country. The previous three editions saw over 5.8 lakh educational institutions and more than 73,000 villages declaring tobacco-free, and the fourth edition marks a significant expansion of the initiative, with universities and colleges being the key focus of the campaign. Addressing the gathering, Prataprao Jadhav urged the youth to reject tobacco and other addictive substances and embrace healthy, fulfilling and addiction-free lives. He emphasised that the health and well-being of young people are central to India's aspirations of becoming a developed nation. Highlighting the pivotal role of young people in nation-building, the Minister said that India's youth are its greatest strength and that their energy, talent, creativity and determination will shape the country's future. He stressed that protecting the younger generation from tobacco and addiction is both a public health imperative and a national responsibility. The Minister drew attention to the serious health consequences of tobacco consumption, noting that tobacco smoke contains more than 7,000 chemicals, including numerous toxic and cancer-causing substances, which can severely damage different organs of the body. Referring to the achievements of the previous three editions, the Minister highlighted that over 5.8 lakh educational institutions and more than 73,000 villages have been declared tobacco-free. Prataprao Jadhav emphasised that the campaign must transcend the boundaries of a government programme and evolve into a mass movement driven by the active participation and leadership of young people. New Delhi, Oct 28 (PTI) The Centre has released Rs 77.98 crore in grant-in-aid for 755 projects under its senior citizens’ welfare scheme for the quarter ending September 30, 2026, the Social Justice and Empowerment Ministry said on Wednesday.
The ministry said it has released funds under the Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens (IPSrC), a component of the Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY), for the financial year 2026-27.
Launched in 2021, AVYAY is a flagship scheme of the ministry that promotes “ageing with dignity” and “ageing in place” by ensuring older persons can live with respect, security, and independence.
The ministry said the assistance aims to strengthen service delivery and welfare interventions for senior citizens through institutional care and related facilities.
With India’s senior citizen population projected to reach 23 crore by 2036, the need for comprehensive and accessible support systems is growing. The scheme seeks to address this demographic challenge by strengthening institutional mechanisms and encouraging community participation, it said.
According to the 2011 Census, India had 10.38 crore people aged 60 years and above, including 5.11 crore males and 5.27 crore females.
The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) highlights functional limitations among a substantial proportion of older persons, underscoring the need for reliable care, healthcare services and community-based support, the ministry said.
Increasing urbanisation, migration and the growth of nuclear households are also changing traditional family support structures, making institutional and community-based care increasingly important for senior citizens, it added.
AVYAY subsumed and expanded the earlier National Action Plan for Senior Citizens (NAPSrC), bringing multiple interventions for older persons under a unified scheme.
The scheme aims to provide shelter, food, healthcare and recreational services while strengthening the capacities of governments, non-governmental organisations, local bodies and communities to support older persons.
The “ageing in place” approach promotes an environment where senior citizens can continue living safely in their homes and communities, supported by suitable home modifications and specialised community-based services where needed, the ministry said.

sum.text:
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has released a list of 543 brands of anti cancer medicines with their revised Maximum Retail Price (MRP). The revised MRPs will be effective from 9th of next month. The revised price list reflects the information submitted by companies up to 27th of this month and it will be updated as and when manufacturers submit their revised prices of non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
According to the official release by the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, several key anti-cancer brands have seen steep price drops. RPG Life Sciences Limited Fulbreca will see its MRP reduced from over twenty six thousand rupees to five thousand 49 rupees, while Abbott Healthcare Private Limited’s BEVACIZAB rate has been cut from over 21 thousand 767 to nearly five thousand 930 rupees.
The revision in prices comes amid NPPA’s announcement on 17th October of Trade Margin Rationalisation for 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in the public interest, aimed at curbing excessive trade margins, making cancer treatment more affordable, and improving access to anti-cancer medicines.

sum.text:
A new species of electric ray fish has been discovered from the deep waters of southeastern Arabian Sea in the northern Indian Ocean, according to the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI). This is the first confirmed record of the genus Tetronarce in the northern Indian Ocean, shedding light on the poorly explored biodiversity of India's deep-sea ecosystems, the ZSI further said. Electric rays, like their bigger sibling manta ray, are cartilaginous fish. They are slow moving bottom-dwellers that live on sandy or muddy seabeds. These fish can generate electric shocks ranging from eight to 220 volts to stun preys and ward off threats.
The discovery was part of a research carried out by the Ministry of Earth Sciences' Deep Ocean Mission project. It has been published in the international taxonomy journal Zootaxa.
"Deep-sea marine habitats remain among the most difficult ecosystems to study," the research team said in a statement.

sum.text:
New Delhi [India], October 28 (ANI): External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar will undertake a diplomatic tour to the United States and the Caribbean to participate in high-level multilateral summits and bilateral discussions, the Ministry of External Affairs announced on Wednesday. Speaking during a biweekly press briefing, MEA Official Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal outlined the minister's upcoming itinerary, confirming his attendance at international summits in both Atlanta and St. John's." The External Affairs Minister will be attending the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting to be held in Atlanta, United States, from 30th to 31st October, 2026," Jaiswal stated. "On the sidelines of this meeting, he will also participate in a QUAD Foreign Ministers' Meeting and also have several bilateral engagements with his counterparts." Following the conclusion of the meetings in the United States, Jaishankar will travel to the Caribbean to lead India's representation at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting." From Atlanta, the External Affairs Minister will be travelling to St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be leading the Indian delegation to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, which is to be held from 1st to 4th of November," Jaiswal said.
Highlighting the focus of the Commonwealth summit, Jaiswal noted that "this time, the theme of the forthcoming CHOGM is accelerating partnerships and investment for a prosperous Commonwealth" and emphasised that "India looks forward to its participation in this particular event." United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Atlanta, Georgia, from October 30 to 31 to host the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, the US Department of State said in an official statement. During the two-day summit, Secretary Rubio will convene foreign ministers representing the world’s leading economies to advance practical cooperation on key shared economic and security challenges, the State Department noted. The United States Department of State said that throughout the ministerial, Washington will work closely with G20 partners to address pressing geopolitical crises that continue to trigger global economic shocks.
According to the official release, the discussions will focus heavily on mitigating disruptions to supply chains, addressing threats to freedom of navigation, and ensuring energy and food security. Underscoring that global security and economic prosperity are "inextricably linked," the State Department…
